objection: Didn’t Jesus say, ‘The Father is greater than I’—and call him the only true God?
answer:
You're right that dating and authorship matter, and I won't wave that away. But the "low-to-high trajectory" thesis runs against the evidence you've already granted: Philippians 2:6–7, widely regarded as an early hymn Paul is quoting rather than composing, already confesses Christ existing in the form of God and taking the form of a servant — that is the highest Christology, attested earlier than Mark's Gospel itself, not a late Hellenistic accretion drifting from Palestine. The direction of travel isn't obviously low-to-high.

Nor is John's Gospel plausibly a corrective pulling an "over-realized" deity claim back toward mere exaltation, since the same Gospel that records "the Father is greater than I" (John 14:28) opens by calling the Word God and ends with Thomas's confession, "My Lord and my God" (John 20:28). What John is doing is distinguishing statements made of Christ according to His incarnate economy from statements made according to His eternal being — the Son sent on mission can rightly call the Father "greater" without implying a lesser nature, just as He can call the Father "my God" according to His assumed humanity while remaining the eternal Word according to His divinity. And the equality-claim isn't floating free of narrative memory either: John 5 preserves a hostile, historically-textured controversy in which the Jews sought to kill Jesus specifically because calling God his own Father was understood as making himself equal with God — that's remembered conflict, not gradual invention.

I'll concede Mark is more reticent than John in style; the Gospels differ in emphasis. But reticent isn't absent, and the whole shape of the witness forces a verdict rather than a comfortable middle where Jesus is a teacher slowly mythologized into a god.

transcript.content: Good point to press me. In John 14:28, Jesus does say "the Father is greater than I," and in John 17:3 he calls the Father "the only true God." But here's where I'd push back: those verses come from the *latest Gospel*, written 60–70 years after Easter by an author who never met Jesus, working in a Greek-speaking community far from Palestine. By then, high Christology was already established in Paul and the hymns you'll cite—so John may be *correcting* an over-realized deity claim, trying to preserve monotheism while still exalting Jesus. The real problem is that the earliest Jesus—Mark's Jesus—barely claims anything explicit about his own nature at all. He proclaims the Kingdom; he doesn't proclaim himself. The trajectory is legendary development: a Jewish teacher gradually *deified* as the decades passed and communities moved further from Aramaic-speaking Palestine into Greek cities where divine-men language came naturally. You're asking me to read John's late theological formulations back into the mind of a first-century rabbi—and that's exactly the move that worries historians.
